arms.predicted: NSGA-II with population=50 and 11 generations will reach 95% of its final 3D hypervolume within the first 200 evaluations (by generation 4), while random search at the same evaluation count will not reach 95% until approximately 300-400 evaluations. The convergence advantage emerges because selection pressure concentrates offspring near the cost-performance Pareto surface.
arms.observed: NSGA-II final HV=8,131,314. Reached 95% threshold (7,724,749) at eval=50 — the very first checkpoint. Convergence trajectory: gen0/eval50=7,984,614; gen1/eval100=8,106,951; gen2/eval150=8,128,888; gen5/eval300=8,131,208; gen10/eval550=8,131,315. Random search also reached 95% threshold (7,722,991) at eval=50 with HV=8,093,142. Both algorithms achieved essentially identical convergence speed (≤50 evals), with no measurable advantage for NSGA-II. The predicted convergence gap (NSGA-II ≤200 vs random ≥300) did not materialize. NSGA-II final HV exceeded random by only 0.02% (8,131,314 vs 8,129,464), within measurement noise.
arms.diagnostic_note: Diagnostic condition (1) confirmed: the Pareto-optimal configuration set per GPU tier is ~40-60% of that tier's configs (not 1-3% as assumed), because batch sizes ≥256 (3 out of 5 options = 60%) achieve tier-optimal metrics while scheduler, routing, block_size, and gpu_mem_util have no effect at rate=50. With ~60% of configs achieving Pareto-optimal objectives per tier, random sampling needs only ~2-3 evaluations per tier to find a representative, covering all 5 tiers within 10-15 evaluations total. NSGA-II's initial random population already saturates the frontier (same failure mode as iter 1, but now in 3D). Crossover between configs from different GPU tiers generates infeasible offspring (TP*inst>8 violations handled by repair), but there is no efficiency gain because the frontier is trivially accessible to random sampling.

arms.predicted: Random search with 550 evaluations will eventually find the same Pareto frontier as NSGA-II (final HV within 2%), but will reach 95% of that HV only after 300-400 evaluations, since each Pareto-optimal tier has approximately 1-3% of configs achieving optimal-for-tier metrics.
arms.observed: Random final HV=8,129,464. Reached 95% threshold (7,722,991) at eval=50 — the first checkpoint — with HV=8,093,142. Convergence plateau reached at eval=250 (HV=8,129,464, stable through eval=550). The predicted 300-400 eval convergence threshold was off by 6-8x. The 8-point Pareto front spans all 5 GPU tiers: rps=37.02/gpu=8, rps=29.74/gpu=4, rps=19.99/gpu=2, rps=17.21/gpu=3, rps=10.92/gpu=1. Final HV within 0.02% of NSGA-II (8,129,464 vs 8,131,314) confirming same frontier was discoverable. The only HV improvement after eval=50 was a small uplift at eval=250 from 8,093,148 to 8,129,464 (+0.45%), likely from finding a slightly better 3-GPU config.
arms.diagnostic_note: The predicted 1-3% per-tier density was wrong by 15-20x. Actual density: ~60% of within-tier configs achieve tier-optimal metrics (any of the 3 largest batch sizes: 256, 512 are sufficient; 64 and 128 fail). With 5 tiers and ~60% per-tier density, a 50-eval random sample has expected coverage of all tiers with high probability (~[1 - (0.4^10)] per tier sampling ≈ 100% coverage). The mechanism confirmed: batch size is the only meaningful within-tier differentiator, not scheduler, routing policy, preemption policy, block size, or gpu_memory_utilization.

arms.predicted: TPE with multi-objective extension will reach 95% of final hypervolume in fewer evaluations than both NSGA-II and random (approximately 100-150 evaluations), because TPE exploits parameter-metric correlations to quickly identify promising regions.
arms.observed: TPE final HV=7,552,260 — 7.1% LOWER than random (8,129,464) and NSGA-II (8,131,314). Reached 95% of its own final HV (7,174,648 threshold) at eval=100 (HV=7,287,566). However, this 95% threshold is relative to a suboptimal final HV, making the 100-eval convergence a misleading metric. TPE achieved SLOWER convergence than random (which hit 95% at eval=50) and converged to a dominated Pareto front. Root cause: Optuna's multivariate TPE fell back to random sampling for conditional parameters (num_instances, routing_policy, admission_policy — which depend on tp and each other), emitting warnings for >400 trials. This caused TPE to miss the tp=2,inst=1 configuration entirely, instead finding tp=1,inst=2 for the 2-GPU tier — which achieves rps=15.6 vs rps=20.0 for tp=2,inst=1. The 2-GPU tier points in TPE's Pareto front (rps=15.6, ttft=81.8 and rps=15.58, ttft=68.8) are dominated by random's discovery (rps=19.99, ttft=62.2) at the same gpu_count=2. TPE also found a degenerate 1-GPU config (ttft=57,514ms, batch=64) demonstrating it explored insufficient batch values for that tier.
arms.diagnostic_note: Diagnostic condition (3) confirmed: TPE's acquisition function concentrated on GPU tier 3 (tp=1,inst=3) which dominated its evaluations at the expense of the 2-GPU tier. This is visible in its 10-point Pareto front: 6 points are at gpu=3 vs 2 points at gpu=2, vs random's more balanced 2 at gpu=3 and 2 at gpu=2. The conditional parameter space (num_instances bounded by tp) is the fundamental incompatibility with multivariate TPE: Optuna's warning messages confirm that routing_policy, admission_policy, and num_instances were sampled independently throughout the 550 evaluations (not just the startup phase), meaning the TPE model never learned the tp→num_instances dependency. The finding that TPE performed WORSE than random (lower final HV by 7.1%) is novel: model-based methods on conditional spaces can be ANTI-helpful compared to uniform random when the conditioning structure breaks the modeling assumptions.

discrepancy_analysis: All three predictions were refuted. The core failure is the same as iter 1 but at a deeper level: the Pareto-optimal configuration set is much denser than the theoretical estimate. Predicted 1-3% per-tier density vs. actual ~40-60% per-tier density (controlled by batch size: 3/5 valid sizes unlock tier-optimal metrics). This makes the search problem trivially easy — random sampling covers all 5 GPU tiers within 10-15 evaluations. Neither NSGA-II's selection pressure nor TPE's density estimation can provide benefit when the target is that easy to hit. An additional novel finding: TPE's multivariate mode actively degraded performance by 7.1% due to conditional parameter space incompatibility. The 3-objective formulation successfully created a non-trivial Pareto frontier (5-8 distinct points across 4-5 GPU tiers), but failed to create a hard enough SEARCH PROBLEM because the frontier is reachable by many configurations, not just rare ones.
